screens.title: Overview
screens.body:
**Topics covered**

- Accessible Tables
- Document Language and Styles
- Color Contrast
- Don't Use Color Alone
- Forms and Field Layout
- Add Benetech's Branded Accessible Letterhead Template to Word
- Creating Accessible PDFs

**Why this matters**

Word Basic covers the everyday habits that matter most. This Advanced module builds on it with what comes up in more formal documents like reports, grants, and anything that goes to the Board or members: more complex tables, document-wide settings like language and styles, color choices, PDFs, and forms. A table-based form, an untagged PDF, or low-contrast text can be just as unusable for someone using a screen reader or with low vision as a document with no headings at all.

It's optional, and recommended if you write reports, grants, or other formal documents - or whenever you'd like to go deeper. Each screen covers one concept: what the problem is, and exactly how to fix it. A short quiz follows once you've been through all of them.

screens.title: Accessible Tables
screens.body:
Tables come with a few specific accessibility traps: using them to lay out a page rather than to show data, merged or split cells breaking the predictable grid a screen reader expects, and missing headers leaving a listener with no idea what a given cell's data actually represents.

**Do:**

- {{answer:word-q6}}Use tables for data only - never to visually position content on the page.{{/answer}}
- Keep the structure simple: no merged or split cells. If your data seems to need them, {{answer:word-q24}}it's better to split it into two or more simple tables{{/answer}}.
- {{answer:word-q7}}Define your headers: click into the table, open **Table Design**, and check **Header Row** if the table has column headings, and **First Column** if it also has row headings.{{/answer}}
- For a long table, also turn on "repeat header row on each page" if that option is available.

**If a table is genuinely complex:** a report's table, with column and row headings and lots of data, asks more of you than a memo's. A few more rules apply:

- {{answer:word-q23}}Never leave a cell empty - type something like "N/A" or "None"{{/answer}}, so a screen reader user isn't left wondering whether a value was skipped.
- Keep alignment consistent down each column.
- Adjust cell padding from **Table Properties > Options** instead of pressing Space or Enter inside cells - the same reason blank lines are best avoided.
- Don't rely on cell shading or color alone to carry meaning - put it in the text as well.

**Keyboard shortcuts:**

- PC: Long-press Alt, then J then T (Table Design), then A for Header Row or M for First Column
- Mac: Shift + Command + / and search for "Repeat Header Rows"

screens.title: Document Language and Styles
screens.body:
Two settings you make once and the whole document inherits: the proofing language, and how your styles look.

**Language**

- Set the correct proofing language under **Review > Language** - {{answer:word-q13}}if it's wrong, a screen reader applies the wrong pronunciation rules to your entire document{{/answer}}.

**Styles**

- {{answer:word-q25}}To change how a kind of heading looks, modify the style itself{{/answer}}: right-click it in the **Home** tab's Styles gallery and choose **Modify**. Every heading using that style updates together, and they all stay real headings.
- Set the spacing you want in the style too (**Format > Paragraph**, then Spacing Before and After), so you never need blank lines to get a gap - the fuller version of the spacing tip in Word Basic.

**Don't:** Reformat headings one at a time by changing the font and size on each. It's slower, and it's easy to miss one.

**Keyboard shortcut (Language):**

- PC: Long-press Alt + R (Review), then U (Language), then L (Set Proofing Language)
- Mac: Shift + Command + / and search for "Language"

screens.title: Color Contrast
screens.body:
Light gray text on a white background can look clean and modern - but if the contrast between text and background isn't strong enough, {{answer:word-q10}}people with low vision or color blindness may not be able to read it at all{{/answer}}.

**Do:**

- Stick to high-contrast combinations, such as dark text on a light background.
- Run the built-in **Accessibility Checker** (covered in Word Basic) - it's very good at flagging contrast issues automatically, and can often suggest a fix.
- When in doubt, check a color pairing with a dedicated contrast-checking tool, such as the one from TPGi.

**Don't:** Use light text on a light background, or otherwise low-contrast color combinations, for body text.

**Keyboard shortcuts:**

- PC: Long-press Alt + H (Home), then FC for Font Color or I for Highlight/Background Color
- Mac: Shift + Command + / and search for "Font Color" or "Highlight"

screens.title: Don't Use Color Alone
screens.body:
Marking urgent tasks in red, or showing status with a colored dot, feels intuitive - but it relies entirely on being able to see and distinguish color. Over 350 million people worldwide are colorblind, and a screen reader never announces color at all, so that information is completely lost to anyone using one.

**Do:** Use color to supplement information, but {{answer:word-q11}}always pair it with a second, non-color indicator - for example, instead of just coloring an urgent task red, also add the word "(Urgent)" or a symbol like an asterisk{{/answer}}. For a status column, use a text label like "Done", "In progress", or "Not started" rather than relying on a green/yellow/red dot alone (and once every status has a label, you can safely delete any color-only legend explaining what the colors meant).

**Don't:** Convey meaning - urgency, status, correctness - through color alone.

screens.title: Forms and Field Layout
screens.body:
Word's built-in **Legacy Form Tools** are not accessible, and should be avoided entirely. Word's newer **Content Controls** (Developer tab) are more accessible than the legacy tools, but this guide still recommends skipping form fields of any kind - legacy or modern - in favor of the simplest possible layout below, one that reads correctly no matter what opens the document. A more subtle problem shows up even without them: placing multiple fields on the same line (for example, "First Name" and "Last Name" side by side, often using an invisible table to align them) creates a confusing reading order. {{answer:word-q9}}A screen reader doesn't see a simple form there - it announces "table with 2 rows and 4 columns" and forces the user to navigate cell by cell to piece the fields together.{{/answer}}

One more thing to check before sharing a fillable document: bracketed placeholder text like "[Type your answer here]" left inside a field. A screen reader reads it exactly as if it were a real answer, which is confusing for anyone filling out - or listening to - the form.

**Do:**

- Skip form fields and tables entirely. Add one clear instruction at the top ("For each item below, enter your information on the line after the label"), then list each field on its own line - for example: "Date:", "First name:", "Last name:", each on a separate line with space to write or type an answer after it.
- {{answer:word-q18}}Delete any bracketed placeholder text before sharing - leave the line blank, or with real content, instead of bracketed instructions.{{/answer}}

**Don't:**

- Use Word's Legacy Form Tools.
- Put more than one field on the same line, or use a table to line fields up visually.
- Leave placeholder text like "[Type your answer here]" in a field once the document is ready to share.

screens.title: Add Benetech's Branded Accessible Letterhead Template to Word
screens.body:
Benetech has two Word templates with accessible styles already set up: Calibri at 14 point, real Heading 1 to 4 styles, and paragraph spacing so you never need blank lines.

- **Benetech Letterhead Template** - for letters. It has the Benetech logo in the header and the address in the footer, and it starts on a normal body line, so you can begin with the date and the person you are writing to.
- **Benetech Accessible Template** - for reports and other documents. It has no header or footer, and it starts on a Heading 1 line - type your document's title there.

**Do:** {{answer:word-q26}}Start each new Benetech document from one of the Benetech templates{{/answer}}. Download the [Benetech Letterhead Template](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/benetech/Accessibility-Training-Modules/main/modules/word-accessibility-advanced/resources/Benetech-Letterhead-Template.dotx) or the [Benetech Accessible Template](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/benetech/Accessibility-Training-Modules/main/modules/word-accessibility-advanced/resources/Benetech-Accessible-Template.dotx) (both are also in your take-home materials), then use them either of two ways:

**Option 1 - run it from your desktop.** Save the file you want to your desktop. Whenever you want a Benetech document, double-click it. If Word opens it in Protected View, click **Enable Editing** - you get a new, unsaved document based on the template. Do not open it from Word's **File > Open**, which opens the template file itself.

**Option 2 - save it to your Custom Office Templates folder.** Then the templates are always there when you start a new document, with no file to hunt for.

**On Windows:**

1. Copy the folder address: {{copy:Copy Windows folder address|Documents\Custom Office Templates}}
2. Open File Explorer, click its address bar, paste with Ctrl+V, and press Enter. The Custom Office Templates folder opens. If Windows says it cannot find it, the folder does not exist yet. Type just `Documents\` in the address bar and press Enter to open your Documents folder, create a new folder there named exactly **Custom Office Templates**, and open it.
3. Move or copy the template files into that folder.
4. In Word, choose **File > New** and open the **Personal** tab. The Benetech templates are there; choose the one you want to start a new document. If it does not appear right away, close and reopen Word.
5. If it still is not under Personal, choose **File > Options > Save**. The **Default personal templates location** box shows the folder Word is looking in - put the file there instead.

**On a Mac:**

1. Close Word, then copy the folder address: {{copy:Copy Mac folder address|~/Library/Group Containers/UBF8T346G9.Office/User Content.localized/Templates.localized}}
2. In Finder, choose **Go > Go to Folder** (Shift+Command+G), paste with Command+V, and press Return.
3. Move or copy the template files into that folder.
4. Open Word and choose **File > New from Template**. Open the **Personal** tab, where the Benetech templates are, and choose the one you want to start a new document.

Two things to know about the templates:

- The Letterhead's logo and address are in the header and footer, which some screen readers skip. If readers need your contact details, also put them in the body of the letter.
- In both templates the **Title** style is set to a tiny 6 point on purpose, as a warning. Use **Heading 1** for your document's title instead.

**Don't:** Copy an old document and delete its content to reuse its look. It carries over whatever was wrong with the old document, and it won't pick up later improvements to the template.

screens.title: Creating Accessible PDFs
screens.body:
Once your document is in good shape, a Word document is itself already the most accessible option you can share. If you do need a PDF, the way you create it matters: a plain "Print to PDF" strips out every bit of accessibility information you built in - your headings, alt text, and table structure all get lost.

**Before you export:**

- Run the **Accessibility Checker** (covered in Word Basic) and resolve everything it reports. A PDF only carries over what is in the Word document, so a clean check there is what makes the PDF accessible.
- Make sure the document uses real Heading styles. The **Create bookmarks using: Headings** option below builds the PDF's navigation panel from them - no headings, no bookmarks, and nothing for a reader to jump between.
- For a long document, add a **Table of Contents** (**References > Table of Contents**) built from those same headings, so readers can also jump to a section from within the text.

**Do:**

- {{answer:word-q16}}Use **Save As** or **Export**, not Print to PDF.{{/answer}}
- **On PC:** File > Export > Create PDF/XPS, then click **Options** and check **Create bookmarks using: Headings** and **Document structure tags for accessibility**, and choose **PDF/A** (or **PDF/UA**) compliant.
- **On Mac:** File > Save As (Shift + Command + S), choose PDF as the format, and select **Best for electronic distribution and accessibility**.

A properly exported PDF from an accessible Word document will carry over most of your work - though a PDF intended for wide public distribution may still need additional tagging beyond what Word's export produces, which is outside the scope of this module.
